title: Working with Data Files
text: These questions check that you can read and write data files, normalize data from different sources, check a merge, and evaluate packages.

tasks.text: Three CSV files with 10, 12 and 9 rows are merged, and the result has 30 records. What does that suggest?
choices: A row was lost somewhere, such as a header treated as data or a blank line dropped wrongly
CSV files always lose one row

tasks.text: What does it mean to normalize data from several sources, and why do it as early as possible?
tasks.answer: Convert everything to one consistent form (same field names, types and formats, e.g. YYYY-MM-DD dates and numbers as numbers). Doing it early means all later steps (combining, sorting, totaling) work on one kind of data and don't need special cases.

tasks.text: An assistant says a package is "popular and actively maintained." Where do you check, and what two facts do you look at?
tasks.answer: Its page on npmjs.com (and its repository): weekly downloads and the date of the latest release (also open issues, maintainers). Assistants recall from training, so claims can be stale.

tasks.text: Write a function usToIso(dateText) that turns a date like 6/5/2027 into 2027-06-05. Then write testUsToIso, which logs usToIso("6/5/2027") and usToIso("12/31/2027").

Download or recreate the three harvest CSV files from the lesson. Start a new chat with your updated learner profile, and ask for a script that merges them and writes a CSV of total kilograms by crop. (1) Paste the reply. (2) Did it follow the new rule, printing counts or totals you can check? (3) Run it and check: 32 records read, 70.9 kg in total, and one crop total of your choice against the harvest table in Objects and JSON's assessment. Report what you found.
tasks.answer: Full credit: notes rule compliance; reports the checks (32, 70.9, e.g. Bean 10.1). Replies vary, so grade the reasoning.
